basis.text: The returns of the two armies in the Official Records (Union 23,049 lost in the revised return; Confederate 20,451 in the editors' compilation of 1889) and Meade's aggregate of a little over 100,000; the strengths of Lee's army rest on Taylor's and Early's readings of the return of 31 May and on Livermore's computations, which are estimates (inferred).

default.label: Side by side: Union 83,289-100,000+ men, 23,049 lost; Confederate 62,000-75,992 men, 20,451-28,063 lost
default.basis_text: Strength and casualties of each army are shown as claims side by side, each with what it counts. Union: effectives engaged by Livermore (83,289) to the aggregate of Meade's most recent return (a lower bound, over 100,000); casualties by the revised return (23,049). Confederate: effectives at Gettysburg by Taylor (62,000) to Livermore's computation (75,992); casualties by the Official Records' compilation (20,451) to Livermore's estimate (28,063). The returns of 1863 are the documented ends; the others are computed estimates.

range.basis: not displayed: this set holds four measures (strength and casualties of each army), so one range would mix them; the label and basis_text give each measure its own range

animation.note: No army total drives the picture: the soldiers instanced follow the printed strength of each unit (DEC-008 item 1) and the army-level figures here are shown as ranges and are not a claim about a unit.

default.note: Strengths and casualties count different things (aggregate, present for duty, effectives, engaged; returned, compiled, estimated); the viewer shows each with its meaning. The plan's web figures have no source and stay selectable.

positions.label: Union: over 100,000 aggregate, a lower bound (the most recent return, Meade's report of Oct 1863)

support.quote: My own army, of which the most recent return showed an aggregate of a little over 100,000

witness.name: George G. Meade
witness.role: Major General commanding the Army of the Potomac

support.note: Meade, report of 1 Oct 1863 (p. 114): the most recent return, while the army lay "in and around Frederick" (no date is stated), showed "an aggregate of a little over 100,000"; he put Lee at "over 100,000 strong, of all arms" (an estimate). An aggregate counts every man on the return, present or not for duty; it is the high end of the Union figures, not the men engaged.

positions.label: Union: 83,289 effectives engaged (Livermore's estimate, 1900, from the returns of 30 June)

support.page_note: printed page not readable in the text layer (no page marks) (p. 102 of the book)
support.quote: Effectives estimated at 93 per cent, of infantry and artillery and 85 per cent, of cavalry 83,289

witness.name: Thomas L. Livermore
witness.role: Compiler of Numbers and Losses; a former Union officer, not a witness of the battle

support.note: Livermore (1900): infantry and artillery present for duty 87,312, less 17 regiments (9,058) not engaged = 78,254, plus cavalry 12,369, taken at 93 per cent (infantry and artillery) and 85 per cent (cavalry): 83,289 effectives. A computed estimate from the returns of 30 June.

inference.step: Livermore takes the present-for-duty returns of 30 June, deducts regiments he judges not engaged, and counts 93 per cent of the infantry and artillery and 85 per cent of the cavalry as effective; the figure is his computation, not a count.

positions.label: Union: about 75,000 fighting men (the Comte de Paris, 1877), or about 81,000 if stragglers are not deducted

support.page_note: printed page 206-207 of Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 5; no page marks in the text layer
support.quote: Meade brought about 75,000 blue-bellies against Lee's 54,000 grey-backs

witness.name: Louis Philippe d'Orleans, Comte de Paris
witness.role: Historian of the war, who served on the Union staff in 1861-62 and was not at Gettysburg

support.note: The Comte de Paris deducts 6,000 stragglers (Union) and 2,500 (Confederate) and both cavalries: about 75,000 against 54,000; with no notice of the stragglers, 81,000 against somewhat less than 57,000. He calls even the larger figures "above the mark".

support.page_note: printed page 206-207 of Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 5; no page marks in the text layer
support.quote: the figures would be 81,000 against [...] what less than 57,000

witness.name: Louis Philippe d'Orleans, Comte de Paris
witness.role: Historian of the war, who served on the Union staff in 1861-62 and was not at Gettysburg

support.note: "If we were to take no notice of the stragglers, the figures would be 81,000 against somewhat less than 57,000"; he adds that these figures "are certainly, on both sides, above the mark".

reason_not_chosen.text: He counts infantry and artillery on the field of the infantry battle, net of stragglers and cavalry; the other figures count a return.

inference.step: The Comte de Paris starts from the returns, deducts the stragglers and the cavalry, and gives the net; the figures are his computation.

positions.label: Union: 58,000 effective, the printed total of seven figures in the council memorandum of 2 July

witness.name: Meade's chief of staff
witness.role: Pencil memorandum found among General Meade's papers, minutes of the council of 2 July

support.note: The council memorandum (p. 74): seven figures and "total, 58,000". It names no corps and does not say what it counts. The seven printed figures add to 59,000, not the printed 58,000 (a discrepancy in the original). Unsigned pencil memorandum found among Meade's papers, indorsed by the chief of staff.

reason_not_chosen.text: The memorandum names no corps and does not say what it counts; its seven figures add to 59,000, not the printed 58,000. It is not shown as the army's strength.

positions.label: Union: 93,693 effectives (the Park Service seminar paper of 2010)

support.quote: Meade fought the battle with 93,693 effectives and suffered a total loss of 22,807 soldiers

witness.name: Matthew Atkinson
witness.role: Park historian, Gettysburg National Military Park (Papers of the 2010 Gettysburg Seminar)

support.note: Atkinson (2010): Meade "93,693 effectives", total loss 22,807 (3,149 killed, 14,501 wounded, 5,157 captured); he gives a note number and no source in the sentence.

reason_not_chosen.text: A modern seminar paper that names no return; the figures it gives for losses (22,807) match no return in the Official Records, which read 23,049.

positions.label: Confederate: 68,352 effectives on 31 May 1863 (Lee's return, as Taylor copied it)

support.page_note: printed page 85 of Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 4; no page marks in the text layer
support.quote: On the 31st May our effective strength as 68,352 ; but one brigade, Pettigrew's, joined the army after this

witness.name: Walter H. Taylor
witness.role: Colonel, Lee's adjutant general, who copied the army's returns at the War Department; articles of 1877 and book of 1906

support.note: Taylor, Lee's adjutant, who "took copies of the original returns" at the War Department: 68,352 effectives on 31 May (the nearest return to the advance); a letter of 1877. Early reads the same return as "a few hundred over sixty-eight thousand".

reason_not_chosen.text: It counts the army before the march (31 May); two cavalry brigades and part of Pickett's division did not reach the field, so the army engaged was smaller.

inference.step: The figure is Taylor's 1877 copy of the return of 31 May; the return itself is not in the volumes read, so the position stands on a witness's report of the return.

positions.label: Confederate: 62,000 effectives at Gettysburg, cavalry included (Taylor, 1877)

support.page_note: printed page 85 of Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 4; no page marks in the text layer
support.quote: reduced General Lee's effective strength at Gettysburg, including Stuart's cavalry, to sixty-two thousand (62,000) men

witness.name: Walter H. Taylor
witness.role: Colonel, Lee's adjutant general, who copied the army's returns at the War Department; articles of 1877 and book of 1906

support.note: Taylor (1877): from 68,352 he deducts the brigades left behind and arrives at 62,000 "including Stuart's cavalry". Early writes of Taylor's figure: "Colonel Taylor puts General Lee's strength at Gettysburg at 62,000 effectives, and his estimate is repeated by General Heth".

inference.step: Taylor deducts from the return of 31 May the brigades that were not at Gettysburg (Corse, Robertson, Jones) and adds Pettigrew; the figure is his reasoning from the return, not a return.

positions.label: Confederate: under 60,000 effectives (Early, 1877; he leaves out the two cavalry brigades left in the passes)

support.page_note: printed page 51 of Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 4; no page marks in the text layer
support.quote: The force with which Gen. Lee invaded Pennsylvania was really under 60,000 effectives

witness.name: Jubal A. Early
witness.role: Lieutenant General, commanded a division of Ewell's corps at Gettysburg; letters of 1877

support.note: Early (letter of 1877): "under 60,000 effectives". In his second paper he explains the difference from Taylor's 62,000: "he includes in his estimate the two cavalry brigades of Robertson and Jones ... whilst I exclude" them.

reason_not_chosen.text: An upper bound ("under 60,000") that differs from Taylor's 62,000 only by the two cavalry brigades left behind; both are estimates from the same return.

inference.step: Early takes the return of 31 May and excludes the brigades that did not reach the field, arriving at less than 60,000; it is his computation.

positions.label: Confederate: 67,000 including all the cavalry (Taylor, 1906): 53,500 infantry, 9,000 cavalry, 4,500 artillery

support.page_note: printed page not readable in the text layer (no page marks)
support.quote: General Lee had at Gettysburg, including all the cavalry, 67,000 men

witness.name: Walter H. Taylor
witness.role: Colonel, Lee's adjutant general, who copied the army's returns at the War Department; articles of 1877 and book of 1906

support.note: Taylor, General Lee (1906), after reasoning from a return of 74,451 effectives: 67,000 including all the cavalry, "of course this number was not available to him at any one time".

reason_not_chosen.text: Taylor's later reckoning (1906) counts all the cavalry, including the brigades that arrived only on 3 July; his own earlier figure (1877) was 62,000.

inference.step: Taylor reasons from the effective return he cites to a Gettysburg figure that includes every cavalry brigade; it is computed.

positions.label: Confederate: 75,000, as Longstreet estimated the whole army at the start of the march (quoted by Oates, 1905)

support.page_note: printed page not readable in the text layer (no page marks)
support.quote: as estimated by General Longstreet, 75,000 men

witness.name: William C. Oates
witness.role: Confederate colonel, writing in 1905 what Longstreet estimated

support.note: Oates (1905): 39 brigades of infantry, 7 of cavalry and 287 guns, "aggregating, as estimated by General Longstreet, 75,000 men". Oates does not give the place in Longstreet.

reason_not_chosen.text: An estimate of the whole army at the start of the march relayed at second hand, by a man who was not on the staff; the returns of Taylor and Early are lower and name their returns.

inference.step: Oates reports Longstreet's estimate of the aggregate of the army at the start of the march; no return is cited.

positions.label: Confederate: 75,992 effectives, or 77,707 engaged (Livermore, 1900: the returns of 31 May and 31 July)

support.page_note: printed page not readable in the text layer (no page marks) (p. 103 of the book)
support.quote: and 85 per cent, of cavalry l 75,992 Deduct losses prior to Gettysburg

witness.name: Thomas L. Livermore
witness.role: Compiler of Numbers and Losses; a former Union officer, not a witness of the battle

support.note: Livermore: infantry and artillery present for duty 31 May 64,167, plus Davis's and Pettigrew's brigades 6,262, plus cavalry 12,346, taken at 93 and 85 per cent: 75,992 effectives.

support.page_note: printed page not readable in the text layer (no page marks) (note 1 to the table, p. 103)
support.quote: Add losses at Gettysburg as above ............ 28,070 Total engaged ......... f ......... 77,707

witness.name: Thomas L. Livermore
witness.role: Compiler of Numbers and Losses; a former Union officer, not a witness of the battle

support.note: Livermore's second computation from the returns of 31 July: the men present then, plus his estimate of the losses at Gettysburg (28,070 with his additions), 77,707 engaged.

inference.step: Livermore computes the effectives from the returns of 31 May (and, separately, of 31 July plus losses) with his percentages; both figures are computed, and the second rests on his own enlarged loss figure. Livermore prints 28,070 for the losses in the note and 28,063 in the table; 77,707 uses 28,070 (49,637 + 28,070).

positions.label: Confederate casualties 22,728: 2,665 killed, 12,599 wounded, 7,464 missing (the Comte de Paris, 1877)

support.page_note: printed page 207 of Southern Historical Society Papers vol. 5; no page marks in the text layer
support.quote: For the Confederates: Killed, 2,665; wounded, 12,599; missing, 7,464. Total, 22,728

witness.role: Historian of the war, who served on the Union staff in 1861-62 and was not at Gettysburg

He says the Confederate figures come from the returns then in his hands; the returns and the date of these figures are not given.

reason_not_chosen.text: A later historian's figure from returns not named, between the Official Records' 20,451 and the estimates; it lies inside the range shown.

inference.step: The Comte de Paris gives the totals as "official figures" from returns he had in 1877, naming none; he adds that about 700 were lost between 3 and 18 July.

positions.label: Confederate casualties 28,063: 3,903 killed, 18,735 wounded, 5,425 missing (Livermore's estimate, 1900)

support.page_note: printed page not readable in the text layer (no page marks) (the Confederate casualties table, about p. 361-362 by the running heads)

witness.name: Edward P. Alexander
witness.role: Confederate artillery officer present at Gettysburg, writing in 1907

support.note: Alexander's table, headed "From Report of Surgeon Guild, excluding slightly wounded and missing": aggregate 2,592 killed, 12,709 wounded, 5,150 missing, 20,451; beside it "Livermore's Estimate 3,903 18,735 5,425 28,063".

support.page_note: printed page not readable in the text layer (no page marks) (note to the Gettysburg table, p. 103)
support.quote: It is certainly within bounds to assume that on the Confederate side the proportion was the average of 1 to 4.8

witness.name: Thomas L. Livermore
witness.role: Compiler of Numbers and Losses; a former Union officer, not a witness of the battle

support.note: Livermore's own method for his Confederate figure: to the 6,802 wounded captured he adds the wounded the Confederate returns did not count and 1,311 killed "to equal the average proportion of killed to wounded" (1 to 4.8), so his 3,903 killed is the return (2,592) plus an assumed 1,311.

inference.step: Livermore adds to the return of 20,451 the 6,026 wounded captured by the Union army above the 770 the returns report left behind, 275 captured in excess, and 1,311 killed assumed so that killed stand to wounded as 1 to 4.8; 20,451 + 6,026 + 275 + 1,311 = 28,063. A computed estimate.

weighing.summary: The totals differ because they count different things and, for the Confederates, because the record itself is incomplete. Union casualties: the Official Records' revised return, 23,049 (3,155 killed, 14,529 wounded, 5,365 missing), replaced Meade's first return of 1863 (23,186); nothing else read is a return, and the plan's 23,055 and 22,822 have no source. Confederate casualties: the Official Records' compilation of 1889 from commanders' reports, 20,451, is known to be short (slightly wounded not counted, one brigade not reporting); Guild's own table is 14,278 killed and wounded; the Comte de Paris gives 22,728; Livermore's estimate adds the wounded the Union army captured and a ratio, 28,063. Strengths: Meade's report gives an aggregate of a little over 100,000 for his army (a return, all men); Livermore computes 83,289 effectives engaged; the Comte de Paris 75,000 net of stragglers and cavalry. For Lee, Taylor copied the return of 31 May (68,352 effectives) and reasons to 62,000 at Gettysburg, Early to under 60,000, Taylor later to 67,000, Longstreet (second hand) 75,000, Livermore 75,992, the Comte de Paris 54,000. The best witnesses disagree, and what each counts differs (return, aggregate, effectives, engaged), so no source or rule separates them: the conflict is irreducible and the default is the set of claims, army by army, with what each counts.
weighing.who: Meade and Guild signed returns of their armies; the Official Records' Confederate return was compiled in 1889 by War Department editors, who call it approximative. Taylor (Lee's adjutant) and Early (a division commander) knew the Confederate returns at first hand and wrote in 1877 to settle the strength; the Comte de Paris, Livermore and Alexander compiled from the returns; Oates relays Longstreet; the Park Service paper of 2010 names no source.
weighing.when: Meade 1 Oct 1863 (and the revised statement in the volume of 1889); Guild 1 Sep 1863; Early and Taylor 1877; the Comte de Paris Dec 1877; Livermore 1900; Alexander 1907; Taylor 1906; the Park Service 2010. By the rule a return or report of the time outranks a compiled table, a table a history, a history a memoir; the Union and Confederate returns are therefore the documented ends, and the later estimates are inferred.
weighing.where: Taylor and Early were with Lee's army and had the returns in hand; Meade wrote from his headquarters. The returns count at different dates: the Union returns of 30 June and 4 July, the Confederate return of 31 May (the nearest to the march; two cavalry brigades and part of Pickett's division did not arrive).
weighing.how_knew: Meade and Guild gave returns made up from corps returns; Taylor copied the original return at the War Department; Early and Taylor reasoned from it to the army at Gettysburg; Livermore computed with fixed percentages (93 per cent of infantry and artillery, 85 per cent of cavalry); the Comte de Paris subtracted stragglers. The Confederate casualty returns exclude the slightly wounded (Lee's order of 14 May 1863, as the New York commission says) and had no return from Jenkins' brigade.
weighing.clock: not applicable: these are counts; the dates are the dates of the returns and reports.
weighing.independence: Groups: Meade's aggregate and his first return (one report), the revised Union return (Livermore and Alexander repeat it), Livermore's computations, Taylor's copy of the return of 31 May (Taylor's two figures, 62,000 and 67,000, and Early's which reasons from it: one line of knowledge, the return), the Comte de Paris, Guild, the Official Records' Confederate compilation (Alexander repeats it), Oates relaying Longstreet, the council memorandum, the Park Service paper. Every figure rests on one line and carries a single_source flag.

source_panel_text: No single figure. Union: 23,049 lost (the revised return); 83,289 effectives engaged (Livermore) to an aggregate of over 100,000 (Meade). Confederate: 20,451 lost (the returns, short) to 28,063 (Livermore's estimate); 62,000 (Taylor) to 75,992 (Livermore) effectives. Each counts something different. 30 other values listed.

owner_note: DEC-008 consequence, reported and not edited: the soldiers instanced follow the printed unit strengths (the plan's Stone Sentinels tables, about 160,000 equipped in all: 91,699 Union and 68,612 Confederate). No documented army figure matches those printed totals: the documented Union figures are 83,289 effectives engaged and an aggregate of a little over 100,000, and the Confederate figures run from 62,000 to 75,992 effectives (68,352 on 31 May). Adding the ends of the ranges gives about 145,000 to 176,000 for both armies, so the drawn crowd of about 160,000 lies inside the range; but the Confederate printed total (68,612) is above Taylor's 62,000 and Early's under 60,000 and the Union total (91,699) is above Livermore's 83,289. The crowd count rests on the printed unit figures, which the sources here neither confirm nor refute for any single unit. This resolution does not change a count.
